title: Oh, How Lovely Is the Evening (round)
description: The evening-bells round in three parts, as a Boston school music reader of 1896 printed it, for 2 to 4 singers: everyone sings the same tune three times, entering six bars apart (tenor and bass an octave lower), and its last line's "ding, dong" rings under the other two.

credits.words: English words anonymous (printed 1896), after the German round "O wie wohl ist mir am Abend"
credits.tune: German round (O wie wohl ist mir am Abend), a folk round after a canon by Karl Friedrich Schulz (died 1850)

licence.words: public domain in the US: the English words are first seen in print in a New York Times report of Frank Damrosch's People's Singing Class (24 October 1892), which says he "wrote these words under the notes" on the blackboard, with no translator named, and then in the 1896 First Reader below, whose words were edited by Nathan Haskell Dole; on the safe side both are counted as possible translators (Damrosch died 1937, Dole 1935). The same words and round, naming no one, are in Songs for Use of Children in Ethical Services (undated, after 1903), No. 16, "Christmas Round", archive.org/details/sochi00slsn (leaf n10)
licence.tune: public domain: a German folk round after a canon by Karl Friedrich Schulz (died 1850); printed here 1896
licence.arrangement: original round setting. Accepted exceptions (singable.py): a round's parts, each the same tune: no voice has a written breath (each sings about 90 seconds straight, going on from "ing," into "is" and "When", from "ing:" into "Ding," and from "dong!" into "O"); the alto, tenor and bass sing the tune's own two notes on "even-" and on "ring-"; the soprano's "Ding, dong" on low E flat stays 5 seconds at the foot of its range; and the bass sings the tune an octave down, so its C on "sweet-" is a tone over the beginner bass range and its middle sits high.
licence.source: The Educational Music Course, First Reader, by Luther Whiting Mason, James M. McLaughlin, George A. Veazie and W. W. Gilchrist, with words edited by Nathan Haskell Dole (Ginn & Company, Boston and London, copyright 1896, printing of 1898), p. 22, "Round", three parts marked I, II and III six bars apart, in F, written here a whole tone lower in E-flat; read from the scan at archive.org/details/educationalmusi05masogoog (leaf n32). The last of them, Dole, died in 1935.
